'''''Lolium temulentum''''', typically known as '''darnel''', '''poison darnel''', '''darnel ryegrass''' or '''cockle''', is an annual plant of the genus ''[[Lolium]]'' within the family [[Poaceae]]. The plant stem can grow up to one meter tall, with [[inflorescence]] in the ears and purple grain. It has a [[cosmopolitan distribution]].

==Growth==
[[File:Lolium temulentum 001.JPG|thumb|left|upright|Habitus]]
[[File:Lolium temulentum MHNT.BOT.2015.34.16.jpg|thumb|''Lolium temulentum'' ([[MHNT]])]]

Darnel usually grows in the same production zones as [[wheat]] and was a serious [[weed]] of cultivation, a [[Vavilovian mimicry|Vavilovian mimic]] of wheat, until modern sorting machinery enabled darnel seeds to be separated efficiently from seed wheat.<ref name=Leroi>{{cite book |author=Leroi, Armand Marie |author-link=Armand Marie Leroi |title=The Lagoon: How Aristotle Invented Science |title-link=Aristotle's Lagoon |publisher=Bloomsbury |date=2014 |isbn=978-1-4088-3622-4 |pages=296–297}}</ref> The similarity between these two plants is so great that in some regions, darnel is called "'''false wheat.'''"<ref>Craig S. Keener, ''The Gospel of Matthew: A Socio-Rhetorical Commentary,'' Wm. B. Eerdmans Publishing, 2009 p.387</ref> It bears a close resemblance to wheat until the ear appears. The spikes of ''L. temulentum'' are more slender than those of wheat. The spikelets are oriented edgeways to the [[rachis]] and have only a single [[glume]], while those of wheat are oriented with the flat side to the rachis and have two glumes. Wheat will appear brown when ripe, whereas darnel is black.<ref>Heinrich W.Guggenheimer, ''The Jerusalem Talmud,''Vol. 1, Part 3, Walter de Gruyter, 2000 p.5</ref>

Darnel can be infected by an [[endophyte|endophytic]] [[fungus]] of the genus ''[[Neotyphodium]]'' and the endophyte-produced, insecticidal [[loline alkaloid]]s were first isolated from this plant.<ref name="Schardl et al 2007">{{cite journal |vauthors=Schardl CL, Grossman RB, Nagabhyru P, Faulkner JR, Mallik UP |year=2007 |title=Loline alkaloids: currencies of mutualism |journal = [[Phytochemistry (journal)|Phytochemistry]] |volume=68 |pages=980–996 |doi=10.1016/j.phytochem.2007.01.010 |pmid=17346759|issue=7|bibcode=2007PChem..68..980S }}</ref>

The French word for darnel is ''ivraie'' (from Latin ''ebriacus'', intoxicated), which expresses the drunken nausea from eating the infected plant, which can be fatal.<ref name=Leroi/> The French name echoes the scientific name, Latin ''temulentus'' "drunk."

==Literary references==
[[File:The enemy sowing darnel seeds.png|thumb|"The enemy sowing darnel seeds" by {{Interlanguage link|Heinrich Füllmaurer|de}} (1526–1546)]]
* [[Aristotle]] mentions darnel in his ''[[On Sleep]]'' amongst a short list of substances which induce sleep.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/sleep.html|title=On Sleep and Sleeplessness|author=<!--Not stated--> |publisher=The Internet Classics Archive |access-date=August 28, 2023}}</ref>
* The ancient Greek botanist [[Theophrastus]] stated in his ''De causis plantarum'' (8:7 §1) that wheat can [[transformation of species|transform]] (''metaballein'') into darnel (''aira''), since fields sown to wheat are often darnel when reaped.<ref> [[Horace]]'s Satire 2.6 refers to “vetch” as the grain eaten by the country mouse while he serves his guest fancier, but that grain is probably not darnel, which is generally toxic to animals and birds as well as humans.</ref>
* Darnel is one of the many ingredients in [[mithridate]], which [[Mithridates VI of Pontus|Mithridates]], the king of ancient [[Kingdom of Pontus|Pontus]], is supposed to have used every day to render him immune to poisoning.
* Darnel was evidently the toxic weed in the [[Parable of the Tares]] in the [[Gospel of Matthew]] in the [[King James Version]] of the Bible, which translated the Aramaic word ''zizania'' as ''tares''<ref>{{cite book |last1=Strong |first1=James |last2=McClintock |first2=John |title=The Cyclopedia of Biblical, Theological, and Ecclesiastical Literature |date=1880 |publisher=Harper and Brothers |location=New York |url=https://www.biblicalcyclopedia.com/T/tares.html |access-date=2026-04-04}}</ref>:

{{Blockquote | Let both grow together until the harvest: and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, Gather ye together first the [[Parable of the Tares|tares]], and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn. | {{bibleverse||Matthew|13:30|KJV}}}}
<!-- BiolConserv137:248. -->
* [[Dionysius of Corinth|Dionysios]], a second-century bishop of [[Ancient Corinth|Corinth]], uses darnel (''zizania'') as a metaphor for the corruptions of his letters caused by "the devil's [[Apostle|apostles]]."<ref>[[Eusebius|Eusebius of Caesarea]], ''[[Ecclesiastical History (Eusebius)|Ecclesiastical History]]'' 4.23.12.</ref>
* Darnel is mentioned in the [[Mishnah]] in [[Kil'ayim (Talmud)|Kilayim]] (1:1) as זונין ({{transliteration|he|zunin}}), similar to the [[Arabic]] زؤان ({{transliteration|ar|zuʾān}}).<ref>Artscroll Kilayim, June 2012</ref>
* The anonymous classic Greek work [[Geoponika]] contains multiple references to darnel (''zizonia'').<ref>See the English translation by Thomas Owen published in 1806 (posted at https://archive.org/details/Geoponica02/page/n2/mode/1up) and the Greek-English Lexicon of Henry George Liddell and Robert Scott (published in 1946 and posted at http://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:1999.04.0057:entry=ziza/nion).</ref>
* In ordering the [[St. Brice's Day massacre]] of all the Danes in England, [[Æthelred the Unready]] observed that "all the Danes who had sprung up in this island, sprouting like cockle amongst the [[wheat]], were to be destroyed by a most just extermination."<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1179/mdh.1986.11.1.1 | volume=11 | journal=Midland History | year=1986 | pages=1–22| last1=Williams | first1=Ann | title='Cockles Amongst the Wheat': Danes and English in the Western Midlands in the First Half of the Eleventh Century }}</ref>
* Darnel is also mentioned as a weed in Shakespeare's ''King Lear''.<ref>{{cite book|chapter=Darnel|title=Natural history in Shakespeare's time|author=Seager, Herbert West|year=1896|page=[https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_EzZaAAAAMAAJ/page/n90 82]|location=London|publisher=Elliot Stock|url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_EzZaAAAAMAAJ}}</ref>
* The 1912 [[Beatrix Potter]] book ''[[The Tale of Mr. Tod]]'' describes a character digging a deep hole for "dog darnel".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.northbanktalent.com/2018/04/20/switch-adult-fiction-childrens-books/|title=Simon Mockler: Making the switch from adult fiction to children’s books|first=Simon|last=Mockler|work=NorthbankTalent.com|date=April 20, 2018|access-date=January 13, 2026}}</ref>
